extraction_style: Deep extraction with short, separated points; topic-level organization; formulas, classifications, numerical values, named scientists, methods and source-specific examples preserved.

topics.title: History and milestones of plant breeding
topics.definition: Plant breeding developed from deliberate selection and artificial crossing into a science based on genetics.

sections.heading: Early milestones
content: Babylonians and Assyrians artificially pollinated date palm as early as 700 BC.
Thomas Fairchild produced the first artificial hybrid in 1717.
Joseph Kolreuter studied extensive tobacco and Solanum crosses during 1760–1766.
Thomas Andrew Knight produced new fruit varieties through artificial hybridization.
Le Coutier reported wheat selection results in 1843.
Patrick Shireff practiced individual plant selection in wheat and oats.
Vilmorin proposed individual plant selection with progeny testing in 1857.
Nilsson and associates refined single-plant selection at Svalöf around 1890.
Johannsen proposed the pure-line theory in 1903.
G.H. Shull's maize work became a foundation for modern hybrid maize breeding.

sections.heading: Major achievements
content: Norman Borlaug developed Mexican semi-dwarf wheat varieties in the 1960s.
Norin 10 supplied the dwarfing gene used in Mexican semi-dwarf wheat.
M.S. Swaminathan introduced Mexican dwarf wheats into India.
IRRI used Dee-geo-woo-gen (DGWG) in development of IR 8 rice.
C.A. Barber and T.S. Venkatraman contributed to sugarcane noblisation.

topics.title: Development of plant breeding in India
topics.definition: Indian plant breeding developed through agricultural departments, research institutes, coordinated projects and agricultural universities.

sections.heading: Institutional milestones
content: Department of Agriculture was created by Government of India in 1871.
Imperial Agricultural Research Institute was established at Pusa in 1905.
The institute shifted to New Delhi in 1936 after earthquake damage in 1934.
Its name changed to Indian Agricultural Research Institute in 1946.
Imperial Council of Agricultural Research was established in 1929.
It became Indian Council of Agricultural Research in 1946.
Indian Central Cotton Committee was established in 1921.
PIRRCOM began in 1956 for cotton, oilseeds and millets.
All India Coordinated Maize Improvement Project started in 1957.
First hybrid maize varieties were released by the project in 1961.
First Agricultural University was established at Pantnagar in 1960.

topics.title: Important scientists and contributions
topics.definition: Several classical breeding methods and concepts are associated with named scientists.

sections.heading: Named contributions
content: Allard and Bradshaw — G × E interaction.
Hull — recurrent selection for SCA.
Jenkins — recurrent selection for GCA.
Davenport — dominance hypothesis.
Flor — gene-for-gene hypothesis.
Johannsen — pure-line concept.
Harlan and Pope — backcross method.
Jones — double-cross scheme.
Jones and Davis — cytoplasmic genetic male sterility.
Hopkins — ear-to-row method.
Lonnquist — modified ear-to-row method.
Blakeslee and Nebel — colchicine.
Goulden — single-seed descent.
Lewis — self-incompatibility classification.
Vavilov — centres of diversity and law of homologous series.
Vilmorin — progeny testing.
Fairchild — first artificial hybrid.
Rimpau — triticale.
Hugo de Vries — mutation.
Shull — heterosis.
Yuan Long Ping — father of hybrid rice.

topics.title: Activities in plant breeding
topics.definition: Plant breeding proceeds through creation or discovery of variation followed by selection, evaluation, multiplication and distribution.

sections.heading: Sources of variation
content: Naturally existing variability includes domestication, germplasm collection and introduction.
New variability can be created by hybridization.
Hybridization includes intervarietal, distant and somatic forms.
Mutation, polyploidy and somaclonal variation create new variability.
Genetic engineering is another source of new variation.

sections.heading: Breeding sequence
content: Selection identifies desirable plants or lines.
Evaluation tests performance and target traits.
Multiplication increases seed or planting material.
Distribution makes the improved material available for cultivation.

topics.title: Concept, nature and role of plant breeding
topics.definition: Plant breeding is the art, science and technology of improving plant genetic makeup for economic use and human benefit.

sections.heading: Core concept
content: Plant breeding is also described as the science of crop improvement.
It changes and improves plant heredity.
N.W. Simmonds described plant breeding as the current phase of crop evolution in 1979.

sections.heading: Role
content: Breeding converts genetic variation into agronomically useful varieties.
The programme is directed by the crop, environment and economic objective.

topics.title: Objectives of plant breeding
topics.definition: Objectives are crop-specific improvements in yield, quality, resistance, adaptation, maturity and other useful traits.

sections.heading: Yield and quality
content: Higher economic yield may mean grain, fodder, fibre, tuber, cane or oil yield.
Yield improvement may use high-yielding varieties or hybrids.
Quality targets include grain size, colour, milling and baking quality in wheat.
Rice breeding may target cooking quality.
Barley breeding may target malting quality.
Vegetable breeding may target nutritive and keeping quality.
Pulse breeding may target protein content.
Oilseed breeding may target oil content.
Cotton breeding may target fibre length, strength and fineness.

sections.heading: Stress and protection
content: Abiotic targets include drought, salinity, heat, cold, frost and wind resistance.
Biotic resistance targets diseases and insects.
Genetic resistance is described as an economical way to reduce losses.
Resistant donor parents can be used from the gene pool.

sections.heading: Plant type and maturity
content: Earliness reduces crop management period and may reduce insecticide use.
Early varieties can permit new crop rotations.
Cotton maturity was reduced from 270 to 170 days in the source example.
Pigeonpea maturity was reduced from 270 to 120 days.
Sugarcane maturity was reduced from 360 to 270 days.
Determinate growth is desirable in mung, pigeonpea and cotton.
Dormancy can prevent pre-harvest germination in greengram, blackgram, barley and pea.
Desirable agronomic traits include plant height, branching, tillering and growth habit.
Dwarf cereals are associated in the source with lodging resistance and fertilizer response.

sections.heading: Special objectives
content: Breeding may eliminate toxic compounds such as neurotoxin in khesari, erucic acid in Brassica and gossypol in cotton seed.
Non-shattering is important in green gram.
Synchronous maturity is desirable in crops requiring repeated pickings.
Photo- and thermo-insensitive varieties expand cultivation into new regions.
Wider adaptability helps stabilize production across environments.
Breeding can create varieties for new seasons; maize can be grown in kharif, rabi and zaid situations.

topics.title: Scope, future prospects and undesirable effects
topics.definition: Future breeding combines classical genetics with molecular biology and biotechnology, while maintaining attention to genetic diversity.

sections.heading: Future prospects
content: Population growth creates continuing demand for crop improvement.
Molecular biology provides sharper tools for breeders.
Biotechnology has enabled field testing of genetically modified crops.
Genes from diverse organisms may improve biotic and abiotic stress resistance.
Plants may be engineered to produce valuable compounds such as pharmaceuticals.
The source cites transgenic Brassica napus producing hirudin as an example.

sections.heading: Undesirable effects
content: Modern improved varieties may be more uniform than landraces.
Reduced diversity can increase vulnerability to new pathogen races.
Uniform varieties may have a narrow genetic base and poorer adaptability.
Shared pedigree parents can create danger of genetic uniformity.
Plant breeding can sometimes create undesirable combinations such as Raphanobrassica and Pomato.
Strong selection for major pests and diseases may increase susceptibility to minor pests or diseases.
The source cites chickpea grey mold epidemics, Karnal bunt in wheat and mealy bugs in Bt cotton as examples.

topics.title: Genetics and cytogenetics in plant breeding
topics.definition: Genetic and cytogenetic principles provide the basis for planned crop improvement.

sections.heading: Important concepts
content: Mitosis and meiosis.
Chromosomes and chromosomal structural changes.
Numerical chromosome changes.
Mendel's laws of inheritance.
Gene interaction, linkage and crossing over.
Pleiotropy, penetrance and expressivity.
Cytoplasmic inheritance.
Polygenic and oligogenic characters.
Mutations and population genetics.
Plant biotechnology.

sections.heading: Mode of reproduction
content: Mode of reproduction determines whether crop populations are mainly homozygous or heterozygous.
Self-pollinated crops such as wheat are generally homozygous.
A homozygous line is therefore a common breeding target in self-pollinators.

topics.title: Vegetative reproduction
topics.definition: Asexual vegetative reproduction produces new plants from vegetative plant parts without gamete fusion.

sections.heading: Natural vegetative structures
content: Tuber — potato.
Bulb — onion and garlic.
Rhizome — ginger and turmeric.
Corm — bunda and arvi.
Sub-aerial stems include runners, stolons and suckers.
Mint and date palm are examples of crops using sub-aerial stems.

sections.heading: Artificial vegetative reproduction
content: Stem cuttings are used in sugarcane, grapes and roses.
Layering, budding, grafting and gootee are used for fruit trees and ornamentals.
Tissue culture permits vegetative multiplication in many plant species.

sections.heading: Breeding significance
content: A desirable plant can be used directly as a variety even when heterozygous.
Desirable mutant buds, branches or seedlings can be multiplied directly.
Vegetative propagation can preserve a selected genotype unchanged.

topics.title: Apomixis
topics.definition: Apomixis is seed formation in which the embryo develops without fertilization.

sections.heading: Types
content: Apomictic progeny is generally genetically identical to the parent.
Facultative apomixis occurs when sexual reproduction can also occur.
Obligate apomixis occurs when sexual reproduction is absent.
Adventive embryony develops embryos directly from nucellus, integument or chalaza.
Apospory produces unreduced embryo sacs from ovular somatic cells.
Diplospory develops the embryo sac from the megaspore, often with modified meiosis.
Parthenogenesis develops the embryo from an embryo-sac cell without pollination.
Gonial parthenogenesis uses the egg cell.
Somatic parthenogenesis uses another embryo-sac cell.
Apogamy develops an embryo from synergids or antipodals.

sections.heading: Breeding significance
content: Apomixis is undesirable when sexual progeny, selfs or hybrids are required.
It is useful for maintaining a desirable genotype unchanged.
Apomictic reproduction can preserve selected varieties without segregation.
Asexually reproducing crops are often highly heterozygous and may show severe inbreeding depression.
Breeding programmes for such crops should avoid unnecessary inbreeding.

topics.title: Sexual reproduction and gametogenesis
topics.definition: Sexual reproduction involves fusion of male and female gametes to form a zygote and creates recombination.

sections.heading: Flower and sporogenesis
content: Perfect or hermaphrodite flowers contain stamens and pistil.
Staminate flowers contain stamens but not pistils.
Pistillate flowers contain pistils but not stamens.
Monoecious species have male and female flowers on the same plant.
Dioecious species have male and female flowers on different plants.
Sporogenesis is production of microspores and megaspores.
Microsporogenesis occurs in anthers.
Each pollen mother cell undergoes meiosis to produce four haploid microspores.
Megasporogenesis occurs in ovules.
A megaspore mother cell produces four haploid megaspores; usually three degenerate.

sections.heading: Gametogenesis
content: Microgametogenesis produces male gametes.
The pollen nucleus forms a generative nucleus and vegetative or tube nucleus.
The generative nucleus divides to form two sperm cells.
The pollen tube enters the ovule through the micropyle.
Megagametogenesis forms the embryo sac from the functional megaspore.
In most crops, three mitotic divisions produce eight nuclei.
The mature embryo sac generally has one egg, two synergids, three antipodals and two polar nuclei forming the diploid secondary nucleus.

sections.heading: Significance
content: Sexual reproduction combines genes from two parents.
Recombination generates many genotypes.
Hybridization uses this variation for crop improvement.

topics.title: Modes of pollination and genetic consequences
topics.definition: Pollination is transfer of pollen from anthers to stigmas; its pattern determines genetic structure and breeding strategy.

sections.heading: Types
content: Self-pollination or autogamy uses pollen from the same flower.
Cross-pollination or allogamy transfers pollen between different plants.
Geitonogamy transfers pollen between flowers of the same plant.
Genetic consequences of geitonogamy are similar to autogamy.

sections.heading: Self-pollination mechanisms
content: Cleistogamy prevents flower opening and promotes complete self-pollination.
Some cereals open only after pollination.
In tomato and brinjal, anthers closely surround the stigma.
In legumes, floral organs enclose anthers and stigma within the keel.
These mechanisms make self-pollination efficient.

sections.heading: Genetic consequence
content: Self-pollination rapidly increases homozygosity.
Self-pollinated populations are highly homozygous.
The source states that self-pollinated species generally do not show inbreeding depression.
Breeding usually aims at developing homozygous varieties.

sections.heading: Cross-pollination mechanisms
content: Dicliny produces separate staminate and pistillate flowers.
Monoecy has male and female flowers on the same plant.
Dioecy has male and female flowers on different plants.
Protogyny means pistils mature before stamens; bajra is an example.
Protandry means stamens mature before pistils; maize and sugarbeet are examples.
Honey bees break the waxy film over alfalfa stigmas and facilitate pollination.
Self-incompatibility prevents successful self-fertilization.
Male sterility produces nonfunctional pollen.

sections.heading: Genetic consequence
content: Cross-pollination preserves and promotes heterozygosity.
Cross-pollinated species may show inbreeding depression.
They often show considerable heterosis.
Breeding may aim at hybrid or synthetic varieties.

sections.heading: Often cross-pollinated crops
content: Jowar, cotton, arhar and safflower are cited as often cross-pollinated.
Cross-pollination can exceed 5% and may reach about 30% in such crops.
Their genetic architecture is intermediate between self- and cross-pollinated crops.

topics.title: Self-incompatibility
topics.definition: Self-incompatibility is failure of pollen from a flower or plant to fertilize compatible female tissue on the same plant.

sections.heading: Classification
content: More than 300 species in about 20 angiosperm families show self-incompatibility in the source.
Heteromorphic and homomorphic systems are recognized.
Homomorphic systems include gametophytic and sporophytic control.

sections.heading: Heteromorphic system
content: Flower morphology differs between incompatibility groups.
Primula has pin and thrum forms; this is distyly.
Lythrum shows tristyly.
In distyly, compatible mating occurs between pin and thrum flowers.
The source gives Ss for thrum and ss for pin.
Pin × thrum produces Ss and ss progeny in equal frequencies.

sections.heading: Gametophytic system
content: Pollen incompatibility is determined by its own genotype.
A single S locus with multiple alleles commonly controls the system.
Pollen carrying an S allele is rejected by stylar tissue carrying the same allele.
Examples include Trifolium, Nicotiana, Lycopersicon, Solanum and Petunia.
S1S2 × S1S2 is fully incompatible.
S1S2 × S3S4 is fully compatible.
S1S2 × S2S3 is partially compatible; about 50% pollen is compatible.

sections.heading: Sporophytic system
content: Pollen reaction is determined by the genotype of the plant producing the pollen.
More than 30 S alleles are reported in Brassica oleracea in the source.
Dominance, codominance or competition can occur among S alleles.
Radish, diploid Brassica and Sinapis are examples.
Reciprocal differences may occur.
Homozygotes can occur as normal members of the system.

sections.heading: Mechanism and breeding use
content: Pollen-stigma, pollen tube-style and pollen tube-ovule interactions can block fertilization.
Gametophytic incompatibility often blocks pollen-tube growth in the stigma or style.
Sporophytic incompatibility commonly acts at the stigma.
Self-incompatibility can be exploited for hybrid seed production.
Two self-incompatible but cross-compatible lines can be interplanted to produce hybrid seed.
Environmental conditions such as high temperature and humidity can reduce incompatibility and increase selfed seed.

sections.heading: Temporary suppression
content: Bud pollination uses mature pollen on immature stigma about 1–2 days before anthesis.
Surgical removal of stigma or style can permit incompatible crosses in some species.
End-of-season pollination may exploit reduced incompatibility late in flowering.
The source reports temperatures up to 60°C inducing pseudofertility in some crops.
X-rays or gamma-rays can temporarily suppress incompatibility in some systems.
Grafting and double pollination have also been reported.

topics.title: Male sterility
topics.definition: Male sterility is production of nonfunctional pollen while female fertility remains functional.

sections.heading: Types
content: Genetic male sterility is usually controlled by a recessive ms gene.
Dominant male-sterility genes are also known, including in safflower.
Cytoplasmic male sterility is controlled by cytoplasm.
Cytoplasmic-genetic male sterility combines sterile cytoplasm with nuclear fertility-restorer genes.

sections.heading: Genetic male sterility
content: ms ms × Ms ms gives about 1:1 male-sterile and male-fertile progeny.
Male-sterile and maintainer lines can be isogenic except at the ms locus.
Male-fertile plants must be identified and removed from the female line before pollen shedding.
This rouging requirement increases hybrid-seed production cost.
The source notes commercial use in castor in the USA and arhar in India.

sections.heading: Cytoplasmic male sterility
content: Cytoplasm is inherited mainly through the egg, so progeny of a male-sterile female remain male sterile.
A recurrent pollinator can maintain the male-sterile A line.
The fertile maintainer is called the B line.
The source associates CMS genes particularly with mitochondria in maize.

sections.heading: Cytoplasmic-genetic system
content: A dominant nuclear restorer gene R restores fertility in sterile cytoplasm.
rr plants remain male sterile with male-sterile cytoplasm.
Rr or RR plants are male fertile.
The system is known in maize, jowar, bajra, sunflower, rice and wheat.
Restorer genes can be transferred through backcrossing.

sections.heading: Hybrid seed production
content: Removal of anthers before fertilization is essential when manual emasculation is required.
Male sterility reduces the need for repeated emasculation.
A, B and R lines are central to CMS-based hybrid systems.

topics.title: Domestication
topics.definition: Domestication is the evolutionary and human-directed transformation of wild plants into cultivated forms.

sections.heading: Key features
content: Domestication begins with selection and cultivation of useful plants.
Selection under cultivation changes plant form, reproduction and adaptation.
Domestication is a major source of cultivated crop diversity.

sections.heading: Breeding relevance
content: Domesticated material provides variation for selection.
Traits associated with cultivation can differ markedly from wild relatives.
Domestication history helps breeders understand available variation.

topics.title: Plant introduction
topics.definition: Plant introduction is bringing crop germplasm from one geographical region into another for cultivation, breeding or evaluation.

sections.heading: Types and purpose
content: Introductions may be primary or secondary.
Primary introduction can be directly cultivated after testing and selection.
Secondary introduction is used as breeding material and may produce improved varieties after crossing or selection.
The source cites popularization of grape cultivation in Haryana and introduction of wheat as examples.

sections.heading: History and institutions
content: Crop plants have been moved into new regions throughout agricultural history.
The source describes an organized Indian plant-introduction programme supported by ICAR from 1956.
NBPGR is identified with national management of agricultural and horticultural germplasm.
The Botanical Survey of India is associated with botanical and medicinal plant resources.

topics.title: Procedure and purposes of plant introduction
topics.definition: Introduction requires procurement, quarantine, evaluation and multiplication before safe use.

sections.heading: Procedure
content: Procurement of planting material is the first step.
Imported material is subjected to quarantine.
Introductions are evaluated for adaptation and useful traits.
Selected material is multiplied after successful evaluation.
Promising introductions can be released as varieties after required trials.

sections.heading: Purpose
content: Introduce useful variation into breeding programmes.
Obtain traits not available in local material.
Provide material for direct cultivation after adaptation.
Support diversification of crops and growing regions.

topics.title: Germplasm collection and conservation
topics.definition: Germplasm collection assembles genetic resources needed for present and future crop improvement.

sections.heading: Collection
content: Germplasm may be collected from cultivated and wild material.
Collections preserve genetic diversity for breeding.
Characterization and evaluation identify useful accessions.

sections.heading: Breeding value
content: Germplasm supplies donors for disease, insect, quality and stress traits.
Exotic and indigenous material can broaden the genetic base.
Conserved accessions support future breeding when new traits are required.

topics.title: Centres of origin and diversity
topics.definition: Centres of origin and diversity identify regions where crops or their diversity are concentrated.

sections.heading: Vavilov concept
content: Vavilov developed the concept of centres of diversity.
Centres of diversity are important sources of genetic variability.
The law of homologous series is also associated with Vavilov.

sections.heading: Breeding significance
content: Regions rich in diversity can provide germplasm for crop improvement.
Wild and cultivated forms in diversity centres can supply useful alleles.
Knowledge of origin helps guide exploration and germplasm collection.

topics.title: Components of genetic variation
topics.definition: Observed phenotypic variation is partitioned into genetic and environmental components for selection decisions.

sections.heading: Variance components
content: Phenotypic variation contains genetic and environmental components.
Genetic variation includes additive and non-additive effects.
Environmental variation can mask genetic differences.
Genotype × environment interaction contributes to observed performance across environments.

sections.heading: Breeding significance
content: Selection is effective when useful variation is heritable.
Partitioning variation helps predict response to selection.
Heritability and genetic advance are used together as selection parameters.

topics.title: Heritability
topics.definition: Heritability measures the proportion of phenotypic variance attributable to genetic variance in a specified population and environment.

sections.heading: Broad-sense heritability
content: Broad-sense heritability is the proportion of total phenotypic variance due to total genetic variance.
H² = Vg / Vp.
The source also expresses estimation using variance components from generations such as VF2 and VF1.

sections.heading: Narrow-sense heritability
content: Narrow-sense heritability focuses on additive genetic variance.
It is especially relevant to response from selection because additive effects are transmitted predictably.

sections.heading: Interpretation
content: Heritability is population- and environment-dependent.
High heritability does not by itself guarantee large genetic gain.
Genetic advance should be considered with heritability.

topics.title: Genetic advance
topics.definition: Genetic advance is the expected improvement in mean genotypic value from selection.

sections.heading: Measures
content: Genetic advance is the difference between mean genotypic value of selected lines and the original population.
Genetic advance as percent of mean = Genetic advance / population mean × 100.
The source classifies GA% mean as low below 10%, moderate at 10–20% and high above 20%.

sections.heading: Joint interpretation
content: High heritability + high genetic advance suggests additive gene effects and effective selection.
High heritability + low genetic advance suggests greater non-additive effects and less rewarding direct selection.
Low heritability + high genetic advance can occur when additive effects exist but environmental effects are large.
Low heritability + low genetic advance suggests strong environmental influence and ineffective selection.

topics.title: Pure-line theory and selection
topics.definition: A pure line is the progeny of a single self-fertilized homozygous plant.

sections.heading: Johannsen's findings
content: Johannsen studied Phaseolus vulgaris, variety Princess.
A market seed lot contained mixtures of larger and smaller seeds.
Selection produced genetically distinct pure lines.
Variation within a pure line was attributed to environment.
Selection within a pure line was ineffective because individuals were genetically homozygous.

sections.heading: Requirements and value
content: Successful selection requires variation.
The variation must be heritable.
Progeny testing helps distinguish genetic from environmental performance.
Pure-line selection is particularly useful in self-pollinated crops.

topics.title: Pure-line selection method: merits and limitations
topics.definition: Pure-line selection identifies superior individual plants from a variable self-pollinated population and evaluates their progenies.

sections.heading: Method
content: Select superior individual plants from a heterogeneous population.
Grow progenies separately.
Compare progenies for uniformity and target traits.
Discard inferior lines.
Test promising pure lines in yield and adaptation trials.
Multiply and release the superior line after confirmation.

sections.heading: Merits
content: Produces highly uniform varieties.
Useful for self-pollinated crops.
Uses existing variability without requiring a planned cross.

sections.heading: Limitations
content: Selection cannot create new genetic variation within an already pure line.
The method depends on available variability.
Narrow genetic base can result if the source population is limited.

topics.title: Hybridization in self-pollinated crops
topics.definition: Hybridization combines desirable genes from different parents to create new segregating variation.

sections.heading: Objectives
content: Combine complementary characters from parents.
Transfer specific resistance or quality traits.
Create transgressive segregants.
Generate variation not present in a single parent.

sections.heading: Types
content: Intervarietal hybridization crosses varieties of the same species.
Distant hybridization uses more remote parents.
Somatic hybridization can combine cells or genomes through tissue-culture approaches.

sections.heading: Basic procedure
content: Select suitable parents.
Synchronize flowering.
Emasculate the female parent where needed.
Bag and protect the female flower.
Apply pollen from the selected male parent.
Tag and record the cross.
Harvest and store F1 seed separately.
Grow F1 plants to confirm hybridity.

topics.title: Emasculation and controlled crossing
topics.definition: Emasculation removes or disables anthers of the female parent before pollen shedding to prevent unwanted selfing.

sections.heading: Methods
content: Hand emasculation removes anthers manually.
Hot-water treatment can kill pollen without removing floral parts.
Alcohol treatment can sterilize or kill pollen in suitable crops.
Suction methods can remove pollen from some flowers.
Male-sterility systems can replace manual emasculation.

sections.heading: Crossing steps
content: Emasculate at the appropriate floral stage.
Bag the emasculated flower.
Collect mature pollen from the male parent.
Pollinate the receptive stigma.
Rebag to prevent contamination.
Label the cross with parent identities and date.
Harvest crossed heads or pods after seed maturation.
Store F1 seed with original tags.

topics.title: Segregating populations and transgressive segregation
topics.definition: F2 and later generations after selfing an F1 segregate for parental genes; some individuals may exceed both parents.

sections.heading: Concept
content: F2 and onward generations are called segregating generations.
Transgressive segregation produces individuals exceeding either parent for one or more characters.
Transgressive breeding exploits these superior segregants.

sections.heading: Main methods
content: Pedigree breeding.
Bulk breeding.
Single-seed descent.
Backcross breeding.
Multiple-cross breeding.

topics.title: Pedigree method
topics.definition: Pedigree breeding selects individual plants and records their ancestry generation by generation until desirable lines become sufficiently homozygous.

sections.heading: Procedure
content: F1 plants are space planted to obtain F2 seed.
About 2,000–10,000 F2 plants may be grown in the source procedure.
About 200–500 desirable F2 plants are selected.
Selected plants are grown as separate progenies in F3.
About 3–5 best plants may be selected from each superior row.
The process continues through F4 and F5; about 20–50 families may be retained at F5.
By F6 many lines become homozygous and uniform.
F7 preliminary yield trials are conducted.
F8–F10 confirm superior lines across trials.
F10–F11 seed is multiplied and distributed.

sections.heading: Merits and limitations
content: Provides information on inheritance.
Allows breeder judgement during selection.
Can recover useful transgressive segregants.
Accurate pedigree records require substantial time.
Large selected material becomes difficult to handle.
Success depends on breeder skill.

sections.heading: Modified form
content: Mass pedigree method combines bulk handling when selection conditions are unfavorable with pedigree selection when conditions are favorable.

topics.title: Bulk method
topics.definition: Bulk breeding advances segregating generations in bulk and postpones intensive individual-plant selection until later generations.

sections.heading: Procedure
content: F1 plants are grown and F2 seed is harvested in bulk.
F2 to about F5 generations are grown as bulk populations with little or no deliberate selection.
F6 is space planted for single-plant selection.
Selected plants are grown as separate progenies in F7.
Preliminary yield testing begins around F8–F9.
Multi-location trials are conducted in later generations.
The source gives F9–F12 as a typical testing and multiplication period.

sections.heading: Merits
content: Simple and convenient.
Inexpensive and less labour-intensive.
No detailed pedigree records are required.
Natural selection operates during early generations.
Useful for studying survival of genes and genotypes.

sections.heading: Limitations
content: May take longer to develop a variety.
Breeder has less opportunity for early selection.
Inheritance information is limited.
Natural selection may favor survival rather than highest economic yield.

topics.title: Single-seed descent
topics.definition: Single-seed descent rapidly advances segregating generations by taking one seed from each plant for the next generation.

sections.heading: Core method
content: The method was suggested by Goulden in 1939.
One seed from each plant is carried forward generation after generation.
Rapid generation advance increases homozygosity without early intensive selection.
Individual plants or lines are evaluated after sufficient homozygosity.

sections.heading: Use
content: Useful when large segregating populations must be advanced quickly.
Reduces space and record requirements during early generations.
Selection is concentrated after advanced generations are obtained.

topics.title: Backcross breeding
topics.definition: Backcross breeding repeatedly crosses a hybrid to one recurrent parent to transfer a specific desirable trait.

sections.heading: Concept
content: The recurrent parent supplies most of the final genetic background.
The donor parent supplies the target gene or trait.
Repeated backcrossing recovers the recurrent-parent genotype.
Selection is made for the desired donor trait during the process.

sections.heading: Use
content: Useful for transferring disease or insect resistance.
Useful for transferring a specific quality or stress trait.
Particularly effective when the donor character is readily identifiable.

topics.title: Multiline concept
topics.definition: A multiline variety is a mixture of genetically similar lines that differ mainly in resistance genes or another specific feature.

sections.heading: Concept
content: Lines in a multiline have a common or similar genetic background.
They differ for specific resistance genes.
A multiline reduces uniform vulnerability to a pathogen population.
The approach was associated in the source with Jenson.

sections.heading: Procedure
content: Develop or identify lines differing for the desired resistance genes.
Select lines that are similar for agronomic background.
Combine the component lines in an appropriate proportion.
Evaluate the mixture for agronomic performance and disease response.

sections.heading: Applications
content: Main application is management of diseases with variable pathogen populations.
Useful where uniform single-gene resistance is vulnerable to pathogen change.

topics.title: Hardy-Weinberg law
topics.definition: Under specified assumptions, allele and genotype frequencies remain constant across generations in a random-mating population.

sections.heading: Law
content: For two alleles A and a, p + q = 1.
Expected genotype frequencies are p² AA, 2pq Aa and q² aa.
Equilibrium means genotype frequencies remain stable from generation to generation.
The law was independently developed by Hardy in 1908 and Weinberg in 1909.

sections.heading: Assumptions
content: Random mating.
No selection.
No mutation.
No migration.
No random genetic drift.
A sufficiently large Mendelian population is implied by the equilibrium model.

topics.title: Forces changing population equilibrium
topics.definition: Evolutionary forces alter allele frequencies and therefore disturb Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.

sections.heading: Forces
content: Selection changes reproductive contribution of genotypes.
Mutation introduces new alleles or changes existing alleles.
Migration moves genes between populations.
Genetic drift changes frequencies through random sampling.
Non-random mating changes genotype frequencies.
These forces are treated as evolutionary forces because they change population genetic structure.

topics.title: Population improvement schemes
topics.definition: Population improvement increases the frequency of desirable alleles in cross-pollinated populations while retaining useful heterozygosity.

sections.heading: Basis
content: Cross-pollinated crops are highly heterozygous and heterogeneous.
Inbreeding should be avoided or minimized because of inbreeding depression.
Individual genotypes are less important than allele frequencies in population improvement.
Selection can be with or without progeny testing.

sections.heading: Classes
content: Selection without progeny testing includes mass selection.
Selection with progeny testing includes progeny selection, line breeding and recurrent selection.

topics.title: Mass selection
topics.definition: Mass selection chooses many superior plants phenotypically and mixes their seed to form the next generation.

sections.heading: Procedure
content: Select plants based on phenotype.
Allow selected plants to intermate or open-pollinate according to the scheme.
Harvest seed from selected plants as required by the method.
Use the selected bulk as the next breeding population.
Repeat cycles when further improvement is required.

sections.heading: Use
content: Simple method for increasing frequency of favorable phenotypes.
Useful when target traits have adequate heritability.
Does not require detailed progeny testing.

topics.title: Recurrent selection
topics.definition: Recurrent selection repeatedly selects superior plants or progenies, intermates selected material and recombines favorable alleles.

sections.heading: Purpose
content: Increase frequency of favorable alleles.
Maintain sufficient genetic variability for continued selection.
Improve a population over repeated cycles.

sections.heading: Forms
content: Recurrent selection for general combining ability targets performance with a tester or reference population.
Recurrent selection for specific combining ability targets performance in a particular cross combination.
The source associates GCA recurrent selection with Jenkins and SCA recurrent selection with Hull.

sections.heading: Cycle
content: Select superior plants or families.
Evaluate progenies as specified by the scheme.
Select the best materials.
Intermate selected plants or families.
Advance the recombined population into another selection cycle.

topics.title: Heterosis and its estimation
topics.definition: Heterosis is superiority of an F1 hybrid over a defined parental or standard reference for a target trait.

sections.heading: Types
content: The term heterosis was first used by Shull in 1914.
Average or mid-parent heterosis compares F1 with the average of two parents.
Heterobeltiosis compares F1 with the superior parent.
Economic, standard or useful heterosis compares F1 with the best commercial or standard variety.
The source describes economic heterosis as the commercially useful estimate.

sections.heading: Formula
content: Mid-parent heterosis (%) = (F1 − MP) / MP × 100.
Superior-parent heterosis (%) = (F1 − BP) / BP × 100.
Standard heterosis (%) = (F1 − standard check) / standard check × 100.

topics.title: Inbreeding depression
topics.definition: Inbreeding depression is reduction in vigor, fertility, yield or related performance caused by increased homozygosity in cross-pollinated populations.

sections.heading: Concept
content: Inbreeding increases homozygosity.
Recessive deleterious alleles become more frequently expressed.
Cross-pollinated crops can show mild to severe inbreeding depression.
Self-pollinated crops generally show much less inbreeding depression.

sections.heading: Relation to heterosis
content: Inbred lines often lose vigor during inbreeding.
Crossing suitable inbred lines can restore vigor in the hybrid.
The magnitude depends on crop, population and genetic constitution.

topics.title: Genetic bases of heterosis and inbreeding depression
topics.definition: The source discusses dominance, overdominance and epistatic explanations for heterosis and inbreeding depression.

sections.heading: Hypotheses
content: Dominance hypothesis explains heterosis through masking deleterious recessive alleles.
Overdominance attributes superior performance to heterozygous advantage at loci.
Epistatic explanations involve interactions among genes at different loci.
No single mechanism necessarily explains all cases of heterosis.

sections.heading: Breeding implication
content: Understanding genetic basis helps guide parent choice and hybrid development.
Genetic divergence and combining ability influence hybrid performance.

topics.title: Physiological basis of heterosis
topics.definition: Heterosis can be expressed through physiological differences in growth, metabolism and resource use.

sections.heading: Manifestations
content: Hybrid vigor may increase growth rate, size and yield.
Differences can occur in photosynthesis, respiration and assimilate production.
Improved physiological efficiency can contribute to superior hybrid performance.

sections.heading: Practical view
content: Physiological expression is a result of underlying genetic differences.
The breeder evaluates the final phenotype and economic performance of hybrids.

topics.title: Commercial utilization of heterosis
topics.definition: Commercial hybrid breeding exploits heterosis by producing seed from selected parental lines.

sections.heading: Requirements
content: Parents must be sufficiently uniform and stable.
Crossing must be reliable and economical.
Hybrid seed production requires effective control of self-pollination.
The hybrid must outperform relevant commercial standards for the target trait.

sections.heading: Systems
content: Male sterility can facilitate hybrid seed production.
Self-incompatibility can also be used in some crops.
Manual emasculation is possible where economical.

topics.title: Development and evaluation of inbred lines
topics.definition: Inbred lines are highly homozygous lines developed through repeated selfing or related inbreeding and used as hybrid parents.

sections.heading: Development
content: Select suitable source populations.
Self-pollinate selected plants repeatedly.
Select uniform and fertile lines during inbreeding.
Evaluate lines for agronomic performance and combining ability.
Maintain superior lines through controlled selfing or appropriate seed-production procedures.

sections.heading: Evaluation
content: Evaluate general combining ability where relevant.
Test specific combining ability through crosses.
Assess yield, quality, resistance, maturity and other target traits.
Discard weak or unstable lines.

topics.title: Composite and synthetic varieties
topics.definition: Composite and synthetic varieties are population varieties formed from selected parents or lines while retaining genetic diversity.

sections.heading: Definitions
content: A synthetic variety is produced by intercrossing selected lines with good combining ability.
A composite variety is formed by combining selected genotypes or varieties and allowing them to intermate.
Both maintain more genetic diversity than a single pure line.

sections.heading: Synthetic production
content: Evaluate candidate lines for combining ability.
Select lines with desirable performance and compatibility.
Intermate selected lines in a controlled scheme.
Bulk and maintain the resulting population.
Evaluate performance across environments.

sections.heading: Merits and limitations
content: Synthetics can maintain useful heterozygosity and broad adaptation.
They may be easier to maintain than commercial single-cross hybrids in some crops.
Performance can decline across generations due to recombination and segregation.
The number and combining ability of component lines influence performance.

topics.title: Breeding of vegetatively propagated crops
topics.definition: Clonal breeding improves crops propagated through vegetative organs and preserves selected genotypes as clones.

sections.heading: Characteristics
content: A clone is a group of plants produced from one plant by asexual reproduction.
Asexually propagated crops may lack seed, have short seed viability or produce seed rarely.
Many are perennials; annual examples include potato, cassava and sweet potato.
Many show reduced flowering or seed set.
They are commonly cross-pollinated, highly heterozygous and may show severe inbreeding depression.
Many are polyploids, such as sugarcane and potato.
Some are interspecific hybrids, including banana and sugarcane.

sections.heading: Clone properties
content: Members of a clone are genetically identical in principle.
Within-clone phenotypic variation is mainly environmental.
Phenotype reflects genotype, environment and G × E interaction.
Clones can be maintained for generations.
Clones may deteriorate through pathogens and mutation.

topics.title: Clonal selection and breeding problems
topics.definition: Clonal selection identifies superior plants and multiplies them vegetatively without fixing the genotype through sexual reproduction.

sections.heading: Selection
content: Select superior individual plants from a variable clonal population.
Multiply selected plants vegetatively.
Test clonal progenies in replicated and multi-environment trials.
Discard unstable or inferior clones.
Maintain elite clones through disease-free propagation.

sections.heading: Advantages
content: Heterozygous genotypes can be preserved.
A desirable plant can be released without homozygosity.
Genetic combinations can be maintained generation after generation.

sections.heading: Problems
content: Disease accumulation is a major concern in vegetatively propagated crops.
Sexual recombination may be difficult because flowering or seed set is poor.
Severe inbreeding depression can limit selfing.
Polyploidy and sterility complicate genetic analysis.
Long generation time is a problem in perennial crops.

topics.title: Breeding records and data collection
topics.definition: Accurate records allow breeders to identify, compare, trace and evaluate large numbers of breeding materials.

sections.heading: Need for records
content: Variety development requires evaluation across environments and locations.
Breeders may handle thousands of strains each year.
Complete and accurate records support identification and decision-making.

sections.heading: Major records
content: Accession records.
Project book.
Sowing or planting plan.
Planting list.
Record book of crosses.
Field book.

sections.heading: Maintenance registers
content: Accession register.
Germplasm bank records.
Descriptive blank register.
Crossing programme records.
Single-plant selection register.
Row test and replicated-row test records.
Preliminary and initial evaluation trial records.
Comparative yield and yield evaluation trial records.
Multi-location trial records.
Quality observation notebook.
Segregating-generation notebook.

topics.title: Accession register
topics.definition: An accession register tracks the identity, source, receipt and evaluation history of germplasm or planting material.

sections.heading: Contents
content: Record receipt date.
Record source and accession number.
Assign the number at the receiving unit.
Maintain a short description of planting material.
Record destination for evaluation.
Record evaluation feedback.

sections.heading: Numbering
content: The source describes accession numbers as serial number plus year of entry.
EC denotes exotic collection.
IC denotes indigenous collection.

topics.title: Cross and selection designation
topics.definition: Designation systems provide unique identifiers for crosses, selections and introductions.

sections.heading: Purpose
content: Identify breeding material through generations.
Connect a selected line to its original cross or introduction.
Prevent loss of ancestry information during large breeding programmes.

sections.heading: Source convention
content: The source describes codes containing programme or material identifiers and year information.
Selection, cross and introduction series numbers are used to trace material.
Correct designation is essential for pedigree and trial records.

topics.title: Wide or distant hybridization
topics.definition: Wide hybridization crosses individuals from different species or genera to transfer useful variation across reproductive boundaries.

sections.heading: Definitions and history
content: Interspecific hybridization crosses different species within the same genus.
Example: Oryza sativa × O. perennis.
Intergeneric hybridization crosses species belonging to different genera.
Example: wheat × rye.
Wide or distant hybridization includes interspecific and intergeneric crosses.
Thomas Fairchild produced the first cited distant hybrid in 1717: carnation × sweet william.
Raphanobrassica was an amphidiploid radish × cabbage hybrid.
Triticale is cited as an intergeneric hybrid with major potential.

sections.heading: Objectives
content: Transfer disease-resistance genes from wild relatives.
Transfer insect resistance.
Transfer drought resistance and cold tolerance.
Improve quality, such as cotton fibre or tobacco leaf traits.
Improve yield in oats, tobacco, maize and sugarcane.
Transfer CMS, earliness, dwarfness or useful morphological characters.

topics.title: Barriers to wide hybridization and their overcoming
topics.definition: Wide crosses are limited by pre-fertilization, post-fertilization and chromosome-related barriers.

sections.heading: Barriers
content: Poor pollen germination or pollen-stigma incompatibility can prevent fertilization.
Pollen-tube growth may be inhibited in the style.
Embryo development may fail after fertilization.
Hybrid sterility can result from chromosome imbalance or poor chromosome pairing.
Genetic incompatibility may prevent normal hybrid development.

sections.heading: Breeding approaches
content: Use appropriate parents and reciprocal crosses.
Manipulate pollination timing.
Use embryo rescue when hybrid embryos abort.
Double chromosome number where fertility requires chromosome pairing.
Backcross useful hybrids to a cultivated parent to recover agronomic background.
Repeated selection can stabilize useful introgressed characters.

topics.title: Applications of wide hybridization
topics.definition: Wide hybridization broadens the genetic base by moving useful genes from related species or genera into crops.

sections.heading: Applications
content: Disease and insect resistance from wild relatives.
Abiotic stress tolerance such as drought and cold tolerance.
Quality improvement in fibre and leaf products.
Yield improvement.
Transfer of male sterility, earliness and dwarfness.
Creation of new amphidiploids or crop types.

topics.title: Mutation breeding
topics.definition: Mutation breeding uses induced heritable variation to obtain useful changes not readily available through existing variation.

sections.heading: Concept and history
content: Hugo de Vries coined the term mutation in 1900.
Mutation means a sudden heritable change other than ordinary Mendelian segregation and recombination.
1927 marked discovery of X-ray mutagenesis by Muller in Drosophila.
Stadler demonstrated X-ray mutagenesis in barley in 1929.
Auerbach and Robson demonstrated chemical mutagenesis using nitrogen mustard.
After 1953, molecular understanding of DNA expanded mutation studies.

sections.heading: Types by genetic basis
content: Gene mutations alter DNA base sequence.
Changes may involve base substitution, deletion or addition.
Chromosomal mutations alter chromosome structure or number.
Structural changes include deletion, duplication, inversion and translocation.
Numerical changes include polyploidy and aneuploidy.
Cytoplasmic or plasmagene mutations affect genetic material in cytoplasmic organelles.

topics.title: Mutagens and mutation induction
topics.definition: Mutagens are physical or chemical agents used to increase mutation frequency.

sections.heading: Physical mutagens
content: X-rays.
Gamma rays.
Other ionizing radiation may be used according to the material and objective.

sections.heading: Chemical mutagens
content: Nitrogen mustard is cited as an early chemical mutagen.
Chemical mutagens alter DNA or chromosome behavior and can create heritable variation.

sections.heading: Treatment material
content: Seeds, buds, pollen, cuttings and other plant materials can be treated.
Treatment dose must balance mutation frequency with survival and fertility.
The source describes irradiation procedures followed by generation-wise selection.

topics.title: Selection after mutation induction
topics.definition: Mutation breeding requires screening and selection across generations because most induced changes are not immediately fixed or useful.

sections.heading: Generation handling
content: Treated material is advanced to produce segregating mutant generations.
M1 plants are generally treated material and mutation expression is evaluated in later generations.
M2 is important for detecting recessive mutations.
Subsequent generations are used to confirm stability and performance.
Promising mutants are evaluated in replicated trials.

sections.heading: Selection
content: Select for the desired phenotype.
Confirm that the character is heritable and stable.
Compare mutant lines with the parent variety.
Test yield, quality, resistance and adaptation before release.

topics.title: Polyploidy breeding
topics.definition: Polyploid breeding changes chromosome number to create new variation, restore fertility or modify plant size and other traits.

sections.heading: Autopolyploidy
content: Autopolyploidy increases chromosome sets from the same species.
Colchicine is used to induce chromosome doubling.
Polyploids may show larger cells and organs.
Limitations include reduced fertility, meiotic irregularity and difficulty in fixation of desirable types.

sections.heading: Allopolyploidy
content: Allopolyploidy combines chromosome sets from different species.
Chromosome doubling can restore pairing and fertility in a sterile interspecific hybrid.
It can stabilize wide-hybrid combinations.
Limitations include complex inheritance and fertility problems.

topics.title: Breeding for abiotic stress resistance
topics.definition: Abiotic-stress breeding develops crop varieties that tolerate environmental stresses such as temperature, water and salinity.

sections.heading: Temperature stress
content: Cold tolerance is important in rice-growing areas such as Gudalur and Cumbum valley.
Artificial low-temperature and freeze tests are available, but single-plant selection is difficult.
Field testing of segregating lines is considered suitable but can be time-consuming.
High temperature can reduce seed set.
High temperature may break male sterility in male-sterile lines.
Leaf-disc heat tests and desiccation tolerance tests are used.

sections.heading: Water stress
content: About 75% of cultivated area is described as rainfed in the source.
Drought escape means completing the life cycle before severe water deficit.
Drought tolerance can occur with high tissue water potential.
Drought tolerance can also occur with low tissue water potential.
Physiological traits include stomatal aperture, photosynthetic rate and root characteristics.
Proline accumulation in leaves can be used as a drought-screening indicator.
Excess-water tolerance is important in tail-end Cauvery delta areas.
Deep-water paddy with long stems is suited to excess water.

sections.heading: Chemical stress
content: Salinity and alkalinity can be screened using in-vitro techniques.
Rice seedlings may be raised in test tubes containing different salt concentrations.
Similar screening principles can be used for pesticide or herbicide tolerance.

sections.heading: Difficulties
content: Screening requires high skill.
Screening is time-consuming.
Artificial stress conditions can be expensive.
Field conditions may not provide the required stress intensity uniformly.

topics.title: Genetic markers: concept and classes
topics.definition: Genetic markers are heritable biological features associated with loci that can track individuals, chromosomes or genes.

sections.heading: Concept
content: Markers can act as genetic tags near genes controlling traits.
Markers occupy defined genomic positions called loci.
Marker quality is commonly assessed by heterozygosity in the population of interest.
Important properties include abundance, polymorphism, locus specificity and reproducibility.
No single marker is best for every application.

sections.heading: Classes
content: Classical markers include morphological, cytological and biochemical markers.
DNA markers include RFLP, AFLP, RAPD, SSR and SNP systems.
Markers support genetic mapping, germplasm characterization, marker-assisted introgression and variety protection.

sections.heading: History
content: Alfred Sturtevant produced an early genetic map in Drosophila using morphological factors.
Genetic markers progressed from morphological markers to isozyme markers and then DNA markers.

topics.title: Classical morphological and cytological markers
topics.definition: Classical markers use visible traits or chromosome features to identify inherited variation.

sections.heading: Morphological markers
content: Examples include leaf shape, flower colour, pubescence, pod colour, seed shape and fruit shape.
They are easy to observe and inexpensive.
They can be used as indirect selection criteria when linked to target traits.
They are limited in number.
They may be strongly influenced by environment.
Some appear only late in plant development.
The source cites semi-dwarfism selection in rice and wheat as an example.

sections.heading: Cytological markers
content: Cytological markers identify chromosome structure and banding patterns.
Q bands use quinacrine hydrochloride.
G bands use Giemsa stain.
R bands are reversed G bands.
They help classify chromosomes and identify chromosome changes.
They support physical mapping and linkage-group identification.

topics.title: DNA markers and ideal marker characteristics
topics.definition: DNA markers detect heritable DNA-sequence differences and provide genotype-level information largely independent of phenotype.

sections.heading: Characteristics of an ideal marker
content: High polymorphism.
High reproducibility.
Clear inheritance.
Genome-wide or suitable genomic distribution.
High locus specificity.
Easy and reliable assay.
Low cost and high throughput where possible.

sections.heading: Applications
content: Genetic diversity analysis.
Linkage mapping.
Gene tagging.
Germplasm characterization.
Marker-assisted introgression.
Marker-assisted selection.
Variety identification and protection.
Selection of favorable recurrent-parent genome in breeding programmes.

topics.title: Major DNA marker systems
topics.definition: DNA marker systems differ in how polymorphism is detected and in dominance, reproducibility, cost and throughput.

sections.heading: RFLP
content: RFLP detects DNA polymorphism using restriction-fragment differences.
It is based on restriction digestion and hybridization.
It is generally reproducible and codominant but technically demanding.

sections.heading: RAPD
content: RAPD uses short random primers for PCR amplification.
The source states that about 5–50 ng template DNA may be sufficient.
Advantages include speed, simplicity and no requirement for prior sequence information.
Main limitations are low reproducibility and dominant inheritance.
RAPD cannot reliably distinguish homozygous from heterozygous bands.

sections.heading: AFLP
content: AFLP combines restriction digestion with selective PCR amplification.
Main steps are restriction, adapter ligation, preselective amplification, selective amplification and gel analysis.
The source gives typical AFLP fragments of about 80–500 bp.
Advantages include high genomic abundance and many polymorphic bands per reaction.
Limitations include dominant scoring and technical demands.

sections.heading: SSR and SNP
content: SSR markers are based on variation in repeat number at microsatellite loci.
SSRs are highly useful because of polymorphism and locus specificity.
SNP markers detect single-nucleotide differences.
SNPs can support high-throughput genotyping and genomic applications.

topics.title: Marker-assisted selection (MAS)
topics.definition: MAS integrates DNA-marker detection with conventional breeding to select plants carrying desired alleles.

sections.heading: Procedure
content: Select parents in which at least one parent carries the marker allele for the desired trait.
Grow F1 and use markers to confirm hybrids or remove false hybrids.
Screen F2 individuals and retain plants carrying desired marker alleles.
Screen F2:3 rows and select plants with required marker alleles plus desirable phenotypes.
Continue marker screening in F4 and F5.
Bulk best lines around F4:5 or F5:6 using marker and phenotypic information.
Conduct yield, quality, resistance and other performance trials.

sections.heading: Important considerations
content: Phenotypic selection remains useful when the trait can be evaluated reliably.
A marker does not guarantee expression of the target trait.
Marker–QTL association may vary across environments.
Genetic background can affect QTL expression.
QTL × environment, QTL × QTL and QTL × genetic-background interactions should be considered.

sections.heading: When MAS is especially useful
content: Target traits expressed late in plant development.
Recessive target genes.
Traits requiring special or difficult screening conditions.
Traits with strong environmental variability.
Pyramiding several unlinked genes for durable disease or insect resistance.

topics.title: Intellectual property and major forms of protection
topics.definition: Intellectual property protects creations of the mind and can provide recognition or economic rights under law.

sections.heading: Forms
content: IP is intangible and must be expressed in a discernible form to be protectable.
Examples include patents, trademarks, copyrights, trade secrets, geographical indications and plant varieties.
Copyright protects literary and artistic works and related rights.
Industrial property includes distinctive signs and technology-related rights.

sections.heading: Distinctive signs
content: Trademarks distinguish goods or services of one enterprise from another.
Geographical indications identify goods associated with a specific geographical origin and its characteristics.

sections.heading: Technology-related protection
content: Patents protect inventions.
Industrial designs protect ornamental or aesthetic aspects of articles.
Trade secrets protect confidential information with commercial value.

topics.title: Patent criteria and plant-variety registration criteria
topics.definition: A patent gives an exclusive right for an invention for a limited period when statutory criteria are satisfied.

sections.heading: Patent criteria
content: Novelty means the invention is not known in prior art.
Non-obviousness means the invention involves an inventive step.
Usefulness means it has industrial application.

sections.heading: Plant variety criteria
content: For PPV&FR registration, varieties must satisfy distinctiveness, uniformity and stability (DUS) criteria.
Distinctiveness means the variety differs from previously known varieties.
Uniformity means essential traits are sufficiently consistent among plants.
Stability means essential characteristics remain after reproduction.

sections.heading: Purpose
content: Patent protection is intended to stimulate innovation and research investment.
Publication of patent information provides technical information while granting limited exclusive rights.

topics.title: Plant variety protection in India
topics.definition: India adopted a sui generis plant-variety protection system through the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001.

sections.heading: Legal framework
content: TRIPS requires WTO members to protect plant varieties through patents or an effective sui generis system under Article 27.3(b).
India adopted a sui generis approach.
The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act came into force in 2001.
The source states that the Act covers almost all plants except microorganisms.

sections.heading: Breeders and researchers
content: Registered breeders receive exclusive rights to produce, sell, market, distribute, import or export the variety under Section 28(1).
The breeder's rights can pass to a successor, agent or licensee.
Researchers may use protected varieties for research under Section 30.
A protected variety can serve as an initial source for developing other varieties.
Authorization is required when repeated use as a parental line is necessary for commercial production of the new variety.

sections.heading: Protection duration
content: Trees and vines: 18 years from registration in the source table.
Other crops: 15 years from registration.
Extant notified varieties: 15 years from notification under the Seeds Act, 1966.

topics.title: Farmers' rights under plant-variety protection
topics.definition: The source describes farmer-oriented rights intended to recognize conservation, use and contribution of agricultural genetic resources.

sections.heading: Rights listed in the source
content: Farmers may save, use, reuse, exchange and sell farm produce including seed of registered varieties, subject to the Act's provisions.
Farmers can claim compensation if a registered variety fails to perform as represented at registration.
Farmers are exempted from certain registration and proceeding fees described in the source.
A farmer group or community can register a variety evolved, cultivated and conserved by them.
Farmers may seek benefit sharing when their genetic material contributes to a new registered variety.
Compulsory licensing may be sought when a registered variety is unavailable to farmers at a reasonable price.
The source describes protection from innocent infringement where lack of awareness is established.
Farmers and communities may receive recognition or rewards when conserved material contributes genes to registered varieties.

topics.title: Participatory plant breeding
topics.definition: Participatory plant breeding is breeding carried out collaboratively by breeders, farmers and other stakeholders.

sections.heading: Definition and goals
content: PPB involves collaboration among breeders, farmers, marketers, processors, consumers and policy makers.
The approach is especially emphasized for developing-world farming systems with complex and risk-prone conditions.
Goals include increasing production and profitability.
PPB can target the needs of specific user groups or broader user groups.
It builds farmer skills in selection and seed production.

sections.heading: Participation
content: Breeders can direct research toward the needs of specific farmer groups.
Farmers can help breeders assess trade-offs among traits.
On-farm research evaluates varieties under real farming conditions.
Research can be managed by researchers, farmers or both.
Participatory approaches can improve adoption of innovations.

sections.heading: Activities
content: Identify breeding objectives.
Generate genetic variability and provide plants for breeding.
Select within variable populations.
Evaluate experimental varieties through participatory variety selection.
Support variety release.
Popularize new varieties and management information.
Produce seed.
